The wash is an inline style, so it cannot be overridden from userland. Only the background is dropped: aria-selected is still set on checked rows either way.

components.name: useTableSelectionState
components.description: State management companion for useTableSelection that returns {selectionConfig, selectionState}: selectionConfig (UseTableSelectionConfig<T>) goes to useTableSelection, and selectionState (TableSelectionState) has selectedKeys: ReadonlySet<string>, selectedCount: number, hasSelection: boolean, and clearSelection: () => void, for a bulk-action bar such as TableSelectionToolbar. selectedKeys holds the complete selection, also keys outside the current view, and clearSelection clears all of them. Handles disabled/selectable row filtering for select-all automatically: disabled rows are frozen (preserved across select-all/deselect-all), non-selectable rows are excluded.

props.name: data
props.description: The full data array rendered in the table.

props.name: idKey
props.description: Key extractor: property name or function returning a unique string ID.

props.name: selectedKeys
props.description: Controlled set of selected item IDs.

props.name: setSelectedKeys
props.description: Setter for the controlled selected keys.

props.name: getIsItemSelectable
props.description: Should this row show a checkbox? Non-selectable rows are excluded from select-all.

props.name: getIsItemEnabled
props.description: Is this row checkbox interactive? Disabled rows are frozen: select-all preserves their state.

components.name: useTableSortable
components.description: useTableSortable adds the header sort controls but does not reorder the rows: pass rows that are already sorted as data, sorted by you from the sort state or by useTableSortableState. T is the row type; TypeScript cannot infer it from the config, so it defaults to Record<string, unknown>, which a Table with typed rows rejects: pass it, as in `useTableSortable<Walk>(…)` for `<Table<Walk>>`. When the sort keys have a narrower type than string (a union, or keys that useTableSortableState infers from defaultSort), pass both: `useTableSortable<Walk, WalkSortKey>(…)`. Call it with a config object containing the sort state and callback, and pass the returned plugin to Table via the plugins prop.

props.name: sort
props.description: Current sort state that the headers show; the plugin does not reorder data, so sort your rows from this value (TableSortState<TSortKey>). Ordered array of entries; the first is the primary sort, the rest are tiebreakers. An empty array means unsorted. Direction is the full word: 'ascending' / 'descending', not 'asc' / 'desc'.

props.name: onSortChange
props.description: Called with the next sort state when the user clicks a sortable header; store it and sort your data from it, because the plugin does not reorder rows.

props.name: allowUnsortedState
props.description: Allow cycling back to unsorted. When true: 'ascending', 'descending', unsorted. When false: 'ascending', 'descending', 'ascending'.

props.name: isMultiSortEnabled
props.description: Enable multi-sort via Shift+click. Regular click still replaces the entire sort state.

components.name: useTableSortableState
components.description: Owns a Table's sort state and sorts the rows locally, as a convenience layer over useTableSortable. Pass the rows in, render sortedData, and hand sortConfig to useTableSortable. The hook keeps the state (or reads it from sort and onSortChange when controlled), so header clicks re-sort the rows with no sort code in the component. With isMultiSortEnabled, Shift+click adds tiebreaker columns. For data sorted on a server, use useTableSortable directly and sort where the data lives.

bestPractices.text: Use it when the full data set is in memory, and pass sortedData to Table.
Add a comparator for values whose order is not their string or number value, such as a status rank, and for arrays such as tags, which otherwise have no sort text.
Use it for server-side or paginated-on-server data; the hook only sorts the rows it is given.

components.name: useTableStickyColumns
components.description: Hook that returns a TablePlugin which pins a contiguous run of columns to the start and/or end edge of the table. T is the row type; TypeScript cannot infer it from the config, so it defaults to Record<string, unknown>, which a Table with typed rows rejects: pass it, as in `useTableStickyColumns<Walk>(…)` for `<Table<Walk>>`. Pinned columns get cumulative offsets and a soft, scroll-aware shadow over the scrolling content. An empty config ({}) is a valid no-op that pins nothing.

props.name: startKeys
props.description: Column keys pinned to the start (inline-start / left in LTR) edge: the contiguous run from the first column through the last listed key.

props.name: endKeys
props.description: Column keys pinned to the end (inline-end / right in LTR) edge: the contiguous run from the first listed key through the last column.

components.name: useTableTreeData
components.description: Headless tree plugin for Table: renders nested rows with per-level indentation and expand/collapse chevrons in the tree column (the first column by default), and follows the disclosure pattern: each expand/collapse button carries aria-expanded and, while expanded, aria-controls naming its child rows; indentation shows the hierarchy visually. Composable with the other Table plugins: the canonical plugin order places tree before selection, so the checkbox column lands left of the indented tree column. Feed it the treeConfig from useTableTreeState, or construct the config directly for server-driven or pre-flattened trees. When no row is expandable (flat data), every transform is a pass-through and the table renders identically to one without the plugin. Known limitation: the tree column wraps its cell content, so textOverflow="truncate" tooltips do not apply within the tree column.

props.name: getRowMeta
props.description: Structural meta for a visible row: {id, level (0-based), hasChildren, isExpanded}.

props.name: onToggleItem
props.description: Toggle a row's expansion.

props.name: getRowLabel
props.description: Derive a human-readable row identity for the expander. Astryx combines it with localized expand/collapse wording. Omit it, or return blank text, to keep the generic "Expand row" and "Collapse row" labels.

props.name: hasExpandableRows
props.description: Whether any row in the dataset is expandable. When false the plugin is a no-op: no expanders, no indent, no tree ARIA.

props.name: hasExpandAllControl
props.description: Show an expand-all/collapse-all toggle in the tree column header. Requires isAllExpanded plus onExpandAll/onCollapseAll (all supplied by useTableTreeState).

props.name: isAllExpanded
props.description: Aggregate expansion state across every expandable row, driving the header expand-all toggle. true when all are expanded, false when none are, indeterminate when some are.

props.name: onExpandAll
props.description: Expand every expandable row. Wired to the header control.

props.name: onCollapseAll
props.description: Collapse every row. Wired to the header control.

props.name: indent
props.description: Indent step per level, mapped to the spacing-3 / spacing-4 / spacing-6 tokens.

props.name: treeColumnKey
props.description: Column that carries the indent + expander. Defaults to the first column.

props.name: hasRowClickExpansion
props.description: When true, clicking anywhere on an expandable row toggles its expansion, in addition to the chevron. A pointer-only convenience: keyboard and assistive-tech users toggle via the chevron button. Clicks on interactive cell content (buttons, links, form controls) or a text selection do not toggle. Leaf rows stay inert, and it is a no-op on flat data.

components.name: useTableTreeState
components.description: State management companion for useTableTreeData. Owns the expanded set (controlled or uncontrolled) and flattens nested data into the visible row array; collapsed subtrees are unmounted, not hidden, so the table body contains exactly the visible rows. Returns expandAll/collapseAll helpers, the aggregate isAllExpanded state (true/false/indeterminate) for a header expand-all control, and a ready-to-use config for the tree plugin. Note: because collapsed rows unmount, cell-local React state inside collapsed subtrees is lost on collapse; lift state that must survive.

props.name: data
props.description: Nested data: rows may carry child rows under childrenKey. Flat data (no children anywhere) makes the plugin a no-op, so it can be adopted before the data becomes hierarchical.

props.name: idKey
props.description: Row ID accessor: property name or function returning a unique id.

props.name: childrenKey
props.description: Property holding each row's children array.

props.name: defaultExpandedIds
props.description: Initial expanded row ids for uncontrolled mode. Ignored when expandedIds is provided.

props.name: expandedIds
props.description: Controlled set of expanded row ids. Pair with onExpandedIdsChange.

props.name: onExpandedIdsChange
props.description: Called with the next expanded set whenever expansion changes (both modes). In lazy-loading setups, trigger the children fetch here.

props.name: isItemExpandable
props.description: Should this row show an expander? Overrides the default non-empty-children check; use for lazy loading, where a row is expandable before its children have been fetched.

props.name: sortSiblings
props.description: Sort each sibling group independently during flattening; children always stay directly under their parent. Pass applySort from useTableSortableState to compose with column sorting.

props.name: indent
props.description: Indent step per level (spacing-3 / spacing-4 / spacing-6), forwarded to useTableTreeData.

props.name: treeColumnKey
props.description: Column that carries the indent + expander, forwarded to useTableTreeData. Defaults to the first column.

components.name: useTheme
components.description: Programmatic access to theme tokens for non-CSS consumers like SVG, canvas, Vega, D3, maps, or chart libraries that need values in JavaScript instead of CSS custom property references.

bestPractices.text: Use tokens or token(name) when integrating theme colors into SVG attributes, canvas drawing, chart options, or other non-CSS configuration objects inside React components.
Use resolveThemeTokens(theme, {mode}) for the same token resolution outside React hooks.
Prefer CSS variables or StyleX tokens for ordinary component styling; use this hook only when JavaScript needs token values.
Use data visualization tokens such as --color-data-categorical-blue for chart series instead of arbitrary UI colors.
Hardcode light/dark colors in data visualizations: resolve them through the current theme instead.
Assume the hook reflects every CSS cascade override. It resolves tokens for the current Theme mode; local media-surface overrides and arbitrary external CSS may not be represented.

components.name: useThemeName
components.description: Reads only the active theme name. Use it when code needs to know which theme is on, and does not need tokens or the color mode. It reads ThemeContext when a Theme is above the caller, and otherwise the root theme name on the document element.

bestPractices.text: Use this hook for theme identity, such as picking which icon to show for the active theme.
Use useTheme when the caller also needs token values or the resolved light or dark mode.
Treat null as the name default. Null means no theme name is available.

components.name: useToast
components.description: Hook for showing toast notifications from anywhere in your component tree; it needs no provider or mounted ToastViewport: inside LayerProvider (or a ToastViewport) it uses that viewport, and otherwise the first toast mounts a fallback viewport on document.body with a development warning. Returns the show function itself (not an object): `const showToast = useToast()`; call it with toast options to show the notification.

bestPractices.text: Use for transient success/error feedback that does not require user action.
Set uniqueID to deduplicate toasts from rapid user actions.
For an undo action, pass endContent: <Button label="Undo" variant="ghost" onClick={...} />, and call the dismiss function that showToast returns from that onClick.
Use for critical errors that require acknowledgment; use AlertDialog instead.
Call useToast in the same component that renders LayerProvider; it must be called from a child component inside the provider.

components.name: useTooltip
components.description: Headless hook for hover/focus-triggered tooltips. Builds on useLayer with hover intent, keyboard focus handling, and accessible aria-describedby linking. Use for custom trigger elements that need tooltip behavior without the wrapper component.

bestPractices.text: Use for brief text labels that describe icon buttons, truncated text, abbreviations, or compact controls.
Prefer the Tooltip component for standard wrapping; use the hook when the trigger is not a simple child.

For a toggle-style trigger, have your own button call show() and hide() on each press. Give it aria-describedby and aria-controls set to describedBy, and aria-expanded (true while show() holds the tooltip, false after hide() or onHide), and keep its own accessible name. For an info icon, use InfoTip instead.
Put interactive content inside tooltips: use Popover or HoverCard instead.

components.name: useTranslator
components.description: Returns a translator function that resolves keys against the current locale, provider overrides, and the shipped English fallback catalog. Call inside a component; the returned function can be used anywhere within that component's scope.

components.name: useTreeFocus
components.description: Manages roving-tabindex focus and the WAI-ARIA tree keyboard model. ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Home/End roam linearly over the visible treeitems (skipping disabled ones), while ArrowRight/ArrowLeft carry tree semantics (expand/collapse, move to first-child/parent). Enter/Space activate, and printable characters trigger typeahead.

bestPractices.text: Use for hierarchical tree widgets: wire onToggleExpand to your expansion state and onActiveChange to a single roving tab stop.
Attach both treeRef and handleKeyDown to the role="tree" container element.
Use for linear lists (prefer useListFocus) or 2D grids (prefer useGridFocus); those traversals differ from a tree.

components.name: useTruncation
components.description: Detects whether an element's text is cut off — single-line overflow or clamped to several lines — and gives back the full text, updating when the size or the content changes. Built on a shared ResizeObserver and a shared MutationObserver, so hundreds of table cells create one observer of each kind, and a first measurement runs batched in a microtask after the commit instead of forcing a layout pass per text during mount. Use it wherever a truncated cell should show its full content only when it is actually truncated: compose a Tooltip off isTruncated and fullText instead of always rendering one. Text and Heading build their truncation tooltips on it; reach for it directly when composing truncation feedback into your own component.

bestPractices.text: Render the full-content Tooltip only when isTruncated is true, and read the tooltip text from fullText: a cell that fits shows no tooltip, and the text always matches what was measured.
Apply the matching clamp yourself next to the hook — white-space: nowrap for maxLines 1, -webkit-line-clamp for more — so what the user sees and what the hook measures stay the same shape.
Reuse one useTruncation instance per measured element; the ref callback cleans up its own observers, so swapping elements is safe.
Compare scrollHeight to offsetHeight yourself for clamped text: with -webkit-line-clamp active browsers report the clamped size, which is exactly the case the Range measurement exists for.

components.name: useTypeahead
components.description: Adds APG type-to-focus search to a collection: printable keystrokes are buffered (resetting after a pause), and the first item whose label starts with the buffer (ignoring case, accents, the stroked letters đ ł ø ħ ŧ ƀ and Turkish ı/İ, the same in every locale; a typed accent prefers the exact match) is reported through onMatch. Pressing the same letter repeatedly cycles through the matches rather than filtering deeper. It moves nothing itself; pair it with the collection's own focus management, most often useListFocus or useGridFocus.

bestPractices.text: Wire onMatch to the focus manager you already have (useListFocus.focusItem) instead of moving focus yourself.
Let it see the key event first and fall through to arrow-key navigation only when it returns false.
Pass getCurrentIndex so repeated presses of one letter walk through matches instead of sticking on the first.
Use it on a text input; the field already receives the characters, and typeahead would fight the value.

components.name: VisuallyHidden
components.description: Renders content in the accessibility tree while hiding it visually. Use for accessible names on icon-only controls, aria-live announcement regions, and supplementary screen-reader context. Deliberately has no styling props; the whole point is to stay invisible. `xstyle` is still accepted and ignored, only so code written against 0.7.2 keeps compiling; a planned minor removes it.

props.name: children
props.description: Content exposed to assistive technology while hidden from sight.

props.name: as
props.description: HTML tag to render as. Use a block element for live regions.

bestPractices.text: Use to give icon-only buttons and controls an accessible name that screen readers announce.
Render as a block element (as="div") with aria-live to announce dynamic updates like drag-and-drop or result counts.
Use it to hide content from everyone; it stays in the accessibility tree; use conditional rendering or `hidden` to remove content entirely.
Put interactive controls inside it; the content is not visible and cannot receive pointer input.

tokens.name: --font-family-body
tokens.value: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
tokens.light: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
tokens.dark: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

tokens.value: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

themes.name: neutral
themes.description: Restrained warm grays. Minimal and quiet, so the content stays the focus.

themes.name: butter
themes.description: Warm, creamy yellows with a friendly blue accent. Playful enough for consumer surfaces, soft enough to stay readable.

themes.name: chocolate
themes.description: Warm chocolate theme for Astryx — rich brown palette with Fraunces headings, Albert Sans body, and Lucide icons

themes.name: gothic
themes.description: Deep blue-grays and a signature display serif. Dramatic and editorial, for surfaces that want to be remembered.

themes.name: matcha
themes.description: Earthy greens with a calm, organic feel. Naturalistic and grounded, great for wellness or content-first apps.

themes.name: stone
themes.description: Warm stone and slate, earthy and understated, with just enough character to feel handcrafted.

themes.name: y2k
themes.description: Hot pinks, lime greens, and Poppins. Bubbly, playful, and unmistakably retro.

templates.name: AI Chat Landing
templates.description: Zero-state entry surface centered on a single composer with suggestion chips instead of history, sized for the moment before any content exists. The empty counterpart to a transcript.

templates.name: AI Chat Conversation
templates.description: Transcript of alternating turns carrying mixed rich content inline (markdown, code blocks, collapsible tool-call output) beside a resizable artifact panel that holds generated output while the stream keeps scrolling.

templates.name: Blank
templates.description: Bare scaffold: one heading slot, one empty content region, no navigation and no chrome. The starting point when every other layout imposes more structure than wanted.

templates.name: Canvas Editor
templates.description: Layered artboard workspace: document tabs over a layer rail, a fixed-size frame you zoom on a muted backdrop, and an inspector of position, type, and filter fields that retargets to the selected layer. Objects hold a coordinate rather than reflowing, so moving one never moves another.

templates.name: Centered Hero
templates.description: Symmetrical centered stack (headline, short blurb, paired call-to-action buttons) resting on one wide full-bleed picture, with nothing on either flank competing.

templates.name: Checkout Wizard
templates.description: Multi-step checkout, cart, order, and payment wizard with a running summary that recalculates as answers change. It adapts to its host width, renders the summary first on narrow surfaces, validates every forward path, and completes locally without sending payment.

templates.name: Classic Gallery
templates.description: Uniform grid of equal-ratio media tiles under a centered intro, with filter tabs that narrow the set in place. Regular rhythm, unlike the variable-height masonry variant.

templates.name: Contact Form
templates.description: Flat single-column form mixing control types (text, pill toggles, dropdowns, long free-text) landing on one full-width submit. No steps, no branching, no summary rail.

templates.name: Course Detail
templates.description: Long-form sales page for a single offering, in two columns — read the pitch, then enroll from a sticky rail. The main column holds a preview poster with a fact row, an about block with skill chips, a module syllabus whose sections collapse module by module, an instructor card, reviews with a scored-aspects panel, and a FAQ; the rail holds the price, a self-paced or cohort start picker, and a weekly-pace slider that computes a finish date. The shape for any offering with a curriculum and a purchase panel — a course, class, masterclass, bootcamp, workshop, or training.

templates.name: Service Monitoring Dashboard
templates.description: Always-on analytics with a triage rail: status-colored tiles with sparklines, multi-series time charts over a switchable window, and an independently scrolling alert column that folds into the content when narrow.

templates.name: Funnel & Cohort Dashboard
templates.description: Analytics for sequence and retention questions, pairing two shapes a plain dashboard cannot hold: a staged funnel where each step reads as drop-off against the one before, and a two-axis cohort matrix rendered as a heatmap.

templates.name: Data Dashboard
templates.description: Comparison-heavy analytics behind a persistent filter bar: tiles that each carry an inline sparkline and several period-over-period deltas, then segmented breakdowns underneath. Every number is shown against another number.

templates.name: Portfolio Dashboard
templates.description: Analytics for a value-over-time question: balance and change tiles above a stacked area chart of composition through time, closing on a ranked table of the largest contributors.

templates.name: Project Status Dashboard
templates.description: Status analytics mixing progress and time-axis shapes: a completion donut, a horizontal timeline of dated bars against a today marker, a per-owner table with progress and status, an at-risk list, and a burndown.

templates.name: Executive Summary Dashboard
templates.description: Report-shaped analytics with a prose rail beside the charts: a scorecard of headline numbers with period deltas and status coloring, goal-attainment bars, a trend grid, and a written commentary column that folds beneath the content when narrow.

templates.name: Analytics Dashboard
templates.description: Three-band analytics: a row of headline tiles, then charts, then supporting tables, all re-reading from one global filter bar. Breadth over depth, a summary surface rather than a drill-down.

templates.name: Order Detail
templates.description: Single-record detail in two columns: a summary header with status and actions, a repeating line-item list, a totals block that sums it, and a chronological activity timeline in the rail. The shape for any record holding children plus a history: a customer order with shipping, an invoice, a transaction, or a job.

templates.name: Documentation Design
templates.description: Reference article alternating prose with live rendered examples: an interactive preview, a property table, paired do and don't comparisons, and copyable code blocks.

templates.name: Documentation Technical
templates.description: Reference article ordered as sequential numbered steps with code at each stage, plus callout cards for prerequisites and onward links. A linear walkthrough rather than a browsable reference.

templates.name: Documentation Catalog
templates.description: Reference landing that is pure wayfinding: a banner above a grid of category cards linking into sections, with no article content on the surface itself.

templates.name: Page Editor
templates.description: Two-pane authoring workspace: a side panel with Blocks and Properties tabs beside a live canvas. Add blocks from the Blocks tab, select one to edit it in Properties and see it render immediately, and reorder blocks with move up and move down.

templates.name: File Explorer
templates.description: Hierarchical browser that drills through nested levels as adjacent columns rather than replacing the list each time, with breadcrumb history, switchable list and grid density, and a metadata pane for the selected node.

templates.name: Two-column Form
templates.description: Form split into two columns beneath a hero header: inputs on one flank, a persistent context panel opposite that stays put while the fields scroll. Flat, single submit, no steps.

templates.name: Dialog Wizard
templates.description: Step through a short flow in a dialog, overlay, or popup launched from the page underneath, which stays where it was. Compact step markers and a pinned action row inside a constrained width, rather than the full page a wizard usually gets. Best for two to four short steps — setup, invite, schedule, onboarding — where losing the context underneath would cost more than the flow is worth.

templates.name: Inline Wizard
templates.description: Accordion wizard stacking every step in one column: the active step expands in place while finished ones collapse to a single line carrying their result and a way back in. Steps that run themselves expand into a nested stepper that ticks check by check and halts the column where one fails. Best when later steps depend on what earlier ones decided.

templates.name: Vertical Wizard
templates.description: Multi-step wizard with the steps in a fixed left rail that stays visible while the form scrolls, plus a side panel whose guidance follows the focused field. Suits long or unequal steps carrying uploads, previews, and dense review metadata. As width tightens the guidance drops first, then the rail rotates into a horizontal stepper above the form.

templates.name: Form Wizard
templates.description: Linear multi-step form that moves through one panel at a time, with a horizontal progress track pinned above rather than running down a rail, so every step keeps the full content width for its fields. Only the current step renders, unlike an accordion where each section expands into one long scrolling form. Each advance is validated, and a step left broken stays flagged to jump back to.

templates.name: Gallery Hero
templates.description: Centered stack (headline, short blurb, call-to-action buttons) resolving into a multi-image photo grid rather than one wide full-bleed picture, so the imagery reads as a set.

templates.name: IDE
templates.description: Dense multi-pane workspace of resizable, collapsible regions: a hierarchy tree on one flank, a single read-only code pane in the middle, a docked drawer along the bottom, an inspector opposite. Drag a divider to resize or collapse any of them.

templates.name: Incident Console
templates.description: Dense row queue with an inspector: severity-coded rows grouped by status, a search filter bar, a segmented status control, and a resizable detail pane for the selected row that opens as a bottom sheet on a phone. Rows, not cards, sized for scanning volume.

templates.name: Kanban Board
templates.description: Horizontal lanes of draggable cards where the column itself is the status, so drag and drop between lanes is the state change. Fixed columns, variable-height cards.

templates.name: Card Grid
templates.description: Searchable, browsable card grid with filter tabs and a real empty state: uniform tiles organized by topic, narrowing in place, with no detail surface behind them.

templates.name: Login Card
templates.description: Credential form inside an elevated centered card, third-party provider buttons separated from the fields by a divider, secondary sign-up and legal links beneath.

templates.name: Login Split
templates.description: Credential form filling one half of a two-pane split, full-bleed media holding the other. Same fields as the card variant, but the layout carries brand imagery.

templates.name: Login SSO
templates.description: Progressive credential flow that branches on input: the email domain resolves an identity provider and redirects, with a password path as fallback. Two-stage rather than one form.

templates.name: Basic Login
templates.description: Minimal centered credential form on a plain ground: two fields and a submit, nothing competing for attention. The least-chrome entry surface.

templates.name: Messaging Shell
templates.description: Team messaging app frame: side navigation of channels and direct messages with presence and unread counts, a message stream with a composer, and a thread panel that opens from a message's replies. Dense rows, zero cards.

templates.name: Mixed Gallery
templates.description: Masonry grid of variable-height tiles that pack against each other instead of cropping to a shared ratio, captioned per tile. Irregular rhythm, unlike the uniform gallery.

templates.name: Checkout Form
templates.description: Long sectioned form running beside a summary that stays visible while the fields scroll and recalculates as they change, ending on a terminal confirm of the total. Sections run contact, address, delivery choice, then card details.

templates.name: Product Detail
templates.description: Single-item detail pairing a media gallery with a selection column: variant swatches, a quantity stepper, primary and secondary commit actions, and collapsible specification sections below.

templates.name: Product Gallery
templates.description: Uniform card grid where every tile carries media, title, supporting line, and a price. Browse-to-select only, with no filtering and no detail surface.

templates.name: Settings Dialog
templates.description: Preferences inside a modal container with searchable section navigation, so configuration happens without leaving whatever is underneath. Grouped toggles, live preview of appearance choices, rebindable shortcuts.

templates.name: Settings Panels
templates.description: Preferences split into nav-switched panels: a persistent section list swaps the pane beside it, and rows edit in place rather than opening a separate form.

templates.name: Settings Form
templates.description: Preferences as one continuously scrolling form, sections stacked in order with no navigation between them. The simplest settings shape: everything reachable by scrolling.

templates.name: Shell Nav
templates.description: Application frame combining both navigation axes: a top menu bar with command-palette search over a resizable hierarchy rail, wrapping placeholder content. For when one axis is not enough.

templates.name: Side Nav
templates.description: Application frame with a single collapsible, resizable left rail carrying grouped history and search, wrapping the main content. Vertical navigation only, no top bar.

templates.name: Top Nav
templates.description: Application frame with horizontal navigation only: a centered bar whose items open full-width mega-menu panels, over placeholder content that keeps the entire width.

templates.name: Side Gallery
templates.description: Asymmetric split section: a copy column of headline, supporting text, and links held against a clustered image collage opposite. Deliberately off-balance, unlike the centered hero.

templates.name: Collapsible Table
templates.description: Several tables on one page, each in a collapsible card with its own columns — for groups that do not share a schema, where one table would stand full of empty cells. One time range drives them all, and rows expand into a history chart. Accounts, integrations, sections, sort, expand, or collapse.

templates.name: Comparison Table
templates.description: Transposed matrix that puts candidates in the columns and criteria in grouped rows, with a pinned label column that survives horizontal scroll, columns you can swap or add, and best-in-row marks you can toggle. Compare, comparison, matrix, spec sheet, feature grid, pricing table, benchmark, frozen column, sticky column, or side-by-side.

templates.name: Filterable Table
templates.description: Flat row collection built around progressive filtering: a token bar that escalates into full query syntax, saved views that persist a filter set, column and grouping options, and a resizable detail pane.

templates.name: Grouped Table
templates.description: Row collection bundled into collapsible sections with per-group counts, so a long list reads as a handful of blocks that expand and collapse. Query filtering and a resizable inspector for the selected row.

templates.name: Inbox Table
templates.description: Two-pane message queue: the table indexes a reading pane rather than being the destination, with a divider you drag to resize. Rows stack when the table narrows, not the window; threads read as collapsible messages; replying opens a composer that leaves the list live.

templates.name: Searchable Table
templates.description: Flat table of uniform rows under a block of record-level facts, narrowed three ways at once — a full-text search box, a scope toggle, and per-column popovers — with sortable and filterable columns, per-row hover detail, and totals derived from the visible rows that flag themselves as partial while a filter is on. The shape for one homogeneous list, not nested rows or groups with their own columns.

templates.name: Tree Table
templates.description: Hierarchical table where every parent row rolls up from its children — a code repository whose folders show the newest commit beneath them, beside a detail sidebar and a rendered README. Columns resize, siblings sort within their own level, arrow keys walk the rows, and search prunes the tree to matching branches.

templates.name: Simple Table
templates.description: Flat row collection where columns sort, rows select into a bulk-action toolbar, and each row carries an overflow menu. Sortable but ungrouped, with no detail pane, the baseline shape.

templates.name: Theme Showcase
templates.description: Multi-surface comparison shell: sample product screens (a storefront with an account dialog, checkout, chat, activity and inventory) rendered in the active theme on one responsive canvas. A theme preview and design-system showcase, with an embeddable content view for an existing app shell.

templates.name: Work Item Detail
templates.description: Single work-item detail in two columns: a title with a status selector, a description, a subtask checklist with progress, an attachments block, and a comment and activity feed in the main column, plus a property rail with assignee, dates, labels, and linked items. The shape for any tracked item with children, properties, and a comment history — a task, ticket, issue, story, bug, card, request, or work item.

docs.title: Principles
docs.description: Core design principles and rules for building with the design system.

sections.title: Design Philosophy
sections.body:
A design system that prioritizes consistency, adaptability, and developer experience. Every decision flows from a few core ideas:

- Components over primitives: use components for everything they cover before reaching for raw HTML
- Semantic tokens over hardcoded values: colors, spacing, and radii are named by purpose, not appearance
- Theme-agnostic code: your app code never references specific colors or measurements, so themes and dark mode work automatically
- Open internals: every primitive is exported and composable, so you can build on top of it without fighting it

sections.title: Rules
sections.body:
Eight rules that keep app code on-system.

- Use components for everything they cover
- Page layout is frame-first: pick the shell and budget regions before writing content (see {@link namespace:layout})
- Dense data renders as rows (Table, List/Item), edge-to-edge with dividers; Card is for widgets, galleries, and discrete items; settings groups use Section
- StyleX or Tailwind for custom styling; both are first-class (see {@link namespace:styling})
- Semantic tokens, not hardcoded values (see {@link namespace:tokens})
- CSS custom properties for colors, not hex values
- Form inputs are controlled (value + onChange)
- Use useLinkComponent() for navigation so consumers can plug in their framework router via LinkProvider

sections.title: Styling Approach
sections.body:
The design system supports multiple styling approaches. Every component accepts an `xstyle` prop for StyleX style overrides via `stylex.create()`. For layout and wrapper styling outside of components, use StyleX or Tailwind utilities; both resolve to the same design tokens.

See {@link namespace:styling} for the complete guide with examples.

sections.title: Anti-Patterns
sections.body:
Patterns that break theming, routing, or layout, and what to use instead.

- Inline styles on raw elements. Use xstyle on components
- Hardcoded colors (#fff). Use var(--color-*) or Tailwind semantic classes (text-primary, bg-surface)
- Hardcoded spacing (16px). Use spacing tokens or Tailwind spacing utilities
- Hardcoded <a> elements. Use useLinkComponent() so consumers can swap in their framework router via LinkProvider
- Wrapping every list item or page section in a Card. Decide the frame first; dense data renders as rows (see {@link namespace:layout})
- Badge as decoration. Reserve Badge for counts and enumerated states; use StatusDot or Token for status
- Inventing props. Read component docs first

sections.title: Design Tokens
sections.body: The design system provides semantic design tokens for spacing, color, radius, shadow, typography, and size. Tokens adapt to the active theme and color mode. Run {@link namespace:tokens} for the full reference with all values.

docs.title: Theming
docs.description: How Astryx themes work: wrap your app in a theme, and create or change one (also to make the app denser or roomier, or to change one kind of part) with `astryx experimental theme editor new <name> --like neutral`. The steps follow, then how to publish a theme so other teams can use it.

sections.title: Make or change a theme
sections.body: Use the experimental theme editor: `astryx experimental theme editor new <name> --like neutral`, then `editor set` / `editor how "<what you want>"`, and wire it with `astryx theme add <name>`.

sections.title: Look after each change
sections.body: After each change look at it with `astryx experimental theme editor show <name> --png` (takes pictures of real components): a theme change is not done until you have looked.

sections.title: A denser or roomier app
sections.body: A denser or roomier app is a theme change too, not page code: `astryx experimental theme editor set <name> spacing tight` (or `roomy`), then look again.

sections.title: One kind of part
sections.body: A change to one kind of part (the sidebar, its selected item, the gaps in a form) is a theme change too, not props or styles on one page: `astryx experimental theme editor how "<ask>"` names the `set … --on <part>` line.

sections.title: The values a part shows
sections.body: Before you change a part in a theme, see what it draws now (a card's padding, a button's corners and colors) with the CLI, not the package source: `astryx experimental theme editor show <theme> --on <part>` gives each value, per mode where the modes differ, with the token behind it and whether Core, the base theme or the theme itself sets it. It writes nothing.

sections.title: No app yet
sections.body: `astryx experimental theme preview app <dir>` makes a starter app that shows the theme. How to use and create themes: see Use a theme for applying themes, and Author a theme for creating and customizing them.

sections.title: Share a theme with other teams
sections.body: To publish a theme so other teams can use it, ship it in a package: the package holds the theme in its themes folder, builds it with `{@command theme build}`, and is published like any package. Another team installs the package and runs `{@command theme add <name> --package <package>}`. See {@link generic:add-a-theme}.

sections.title: Wrap your app in a theme
Create a custom theme
Icon sizes
Dark mode
sections.body:
Light, dark, and system modes: {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

```
'--color-accent': ['#0064E0', '#2694FE'],
//                   ^light     ^dark
```

sections.title: Integration themes
sections.body: Install an integration and Astryx discovers its themes automatically. Import one with `{@command theme add <name> --package <integration>}`. Use `theme eject` only for an independent source fork. For the full walkthrough, see {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.description: Add the design system to your project and start building.

sections.title: Quick Start with AI
sections.body:
Paste this into your AI coding tool and let it handle the setup:

```
Install @astryxdesign/core, @stylexjs/stylex, @astryxdesign/theme-neutral, and @astryxdesign/cli in this project, then run `{@command init}` to set up agent docs. Read the generated files to learn the conventions.
```

Then give it a look. Every app gets a theme whether or not anyone picks one, so it is worth one question at setup rather than revisiting screens later that were built around the wrong look:

```
Ask me what look and feel this app should have. Run `{@command theme list}`, install the closest theme package, and run `theme add <slug>`; use `--package` when owners share a slug. Import `themes` and `defaultThemeSlug` from the generated module once and pass `themes[defaultThemeSlug]` to `<Theme>`. Customize with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`. Use `theme eject` only when I ask for an independent source fork. Default to neutral if I have no preference, and show me the result before moving on.
```

sections.title: Install
sections.body:
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.

Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.

```
{@pm install @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli}
```

Then run `{@command init}` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.

```
{@command init}
```

sections.title: Upgrade
Install once, use everywhere
sections.body:
Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never changes what your team and CI get. Keep it in the project as well; that is the recommended setup.

```
{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli --global}
```

Project, global, or both: {@link generic:project-global-or-both}. Everything else about global mode: {@link namespace:global}.

sections.title: Add base CSS and a theme
Add your first component
Customize with StyleX
Example Apps
sections.body:
For a full working project, clone one of the example apps from the repo. These are complete setups with routing, theming, and components wired together.

```
git clone https://github.com/meta/astryx.git
cd astryx/apps/example-nextjs
{@pm install}
{@pm run dev}
```

sections.title: Explore the CLI
sections.body:
The CLI is your reference for components, tokens, templates, and docs. For reliable invocation (especially with AI assistants), add this script to your package.json:

```
"scripts": {
  "astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs"
}
```

Then discover what's available:

```
{@command component}          # list all components
{@command component Button}   # import, usage and props for Button (--detail full adds theming)
{@command docs}               # list all doc topics
{@command template --list}    # available page templates
{@command docs tokens}        # spacing, color, radius reference
```

docs.title: Color
docs.description: Semantic color tokens for surfaces, text, icons, borders, and status indicators.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Colors are semantic: tokens describe purpose, not appearance. Every color adapts automatically between light and dark modes via CSS light-dark(). Themes override the resolved values, so your code never references raw hex colors. Each theme defines its own values: `{@command theme list}` shows the themes that are available.

sections.title: Color Tokens
sections.body: Layered surface hierarchy: body → surface → card → popover. Each level sits visually above the previous one.

sections.title: Use color tokens in StyleX
Best Practices
sections.body:
- Use semantic tokens (--color-text-primary) instead of raw hex values.
- Rely on the surface hierarchy (body → surface → card → popover) for layering.
- Use status colors (success, error, warning) only for their semantic meaning.

- Hardcode hex values, since they won't adapt to dark mode or custom themes.
- Mix accent colors with status colors in the same context.
- Use --color-on-accent on non-accent backgrounds.

docs.title: Spacing
docs.description: Spacing scale tokens for padding, gap, and margin: the rhythmic foundation of design system layouts.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The design system uses a 4px base-unit spacing scale, written in rem so gaps and padding grow with the reader's browser font size the way text does: each step is 0.25rem, which is 4px at the default 16px root. Component gap props accept step values that map to these tokens. The scale provides fine-grained control at the small end (2px, 4px, 6px) and consistent rhythm at larger sizes (multiples of 4px).

sections.title: Scale
sections.body: Fifteen spacing tokens, from 0 to 3rem (0px to 48px at the default 16px root).

sections.title: Usage
Best Practices
sections.body:
- Use component gap props when available; they handle automatic spacing compensation.
- Stick to the scale for consistency. If a value isn't on the scale, reconsider the design.
- Use smaller steps (0.5–2) for tight internal spacing and larger steps (4–8) for section gaps.

- Use arbitrary pixel values outside the scale.
- Mix spacing tokens with raw px/rem values in the same component.

docs.title: Elevation
docs.description: Shadow tokens for visual elevation and inset state rings.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Elevation tokens create depth through box-shadow. Three levels (low, med, high) establish a visual hierarchy for floating elements. Inset shadows provide focus and selection rings for interactive components.

sections.title: Elevation Scale
sections.body: Each level adds stronger offset and spread. Shadow color adapts to dark mode automatically via light-dark().

sections.title: Choosing a level
sections.body:
Pick the level by how far the surface sits from the page, not by how much shadow you want. Elevation encodes stacking order: a higher level means the surface is layered over more of the UI. Use exactly one level per surface, and only raise a surface above `none` when it actually sits above other content.

If two surfaces overlap, the one on top takes the higher level. If a surface does not overlap anything, it is `none` or `low`; never `med` or `high`.

sections.title: The elevation prop
Usage
Best Practices
sections.body:
- Reach for the `elevation` prop on a configurable surface before writing any custom shadow.
- Choose the level by how far the surface sits from the page: `none` when flat/embedded, `low` when in-flow but distinct, `med` when over page content, `high` when over the whole UI. See "Choosing a level".
- Use inset shadows for input focus/selection states; they compose better than outlines.

- Hand-write a `box-shadow` in app code; set the `elevation` prop or read `shadowVars` instead.
- Raise a surface that does not sit above other content; a non-overlapping surface is `none` or `low`, never `med` or `high`.
- Stack multiple elevation levels on the same element.
- Use elevation shadows for decorative borders. Use --color-border tokens instead.

docs.title: Shape
docs.description: Border radius tokens for consistent component rounding, from sharp corners to full pills.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The radius scale uses a semantic naming system: inner → element → container → page. Each level fits a specific context. Themes can multiply the entire scale via a radius multiplier, with --radius-none and --radius-full as fixed anchors.

sections.title: Radius Scale
sections.body: Seven radius tokens, from 0px to 9999px.

sections.title: Concentric Radius
Best Practices
sections.body:
- Use --radius-element for interactive controls (buttons, inputs, selectors).
- Use --radius-container for content containers (cards, panels, dialogs).
- Use --radius-full for pill shapes (badges, tags, avatar status dots).

- Use --radius-page for small elements; it's meant for page-level containers.
- Hardcode radius values; they won't scale with theme radius multipliers.

docs.title: Motion
docs.description: Duration and easing tokens for animations and transitions.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
Motion serves two purposes: it makes interfaces easier to understand, and it makes them more pleasant to use. A panel animating open helps the eye track what changed and where new content sits in the layout. These moments reduce cognitive load and make the interface feel responsive.

At the same time, well-tuned motion gives an application a sense of craft and polish that users notice, even if they can't name it.

The design system provides duration and easing tokens that keep these moments consistent across your application.

sections.title: Duration
sections.body: Nine duration tokens in fast, medium, and slow bands, and `--duration-exit`, the standard dismissal duration, which follows `--duration-fast`.

sections.title: Easing
sections.body: Four easing curves. `--ease-standard` decelerates, for state changes. `--ease-entrance` is for things arriving and `--ease-move` for things moving on screen; a theme's `character` sets both, and at `standard` they equal `--ease-standard`. `--ease-exit` accelerates, for things leaving: it moves off from rest and leaves fast, so the travel stays visible for the whole duration, and it is the same at every `character`.

sections.title: Where Motion Helps
sections.body:
Some parts of the interface benefit from animation. Panels, dialogs, and collapsible sections are disorienting when they appear instantly, so animation gives the eye something to follow. Toasts and notifications need just enough entrance to be noticed without startling. State changes like a switch flipping or a selection highlighting feel more intentional with a brief transition.

The common thread is that these are moments where the user needs to understand what happened.

sections.title: Where Motion Hurts
sections.body:
Table row hovers. List item highlights. Anything the user does dozens of times per minute. Adding perceptible duration to these interactions makes the interface feel like it's catching up to the cursor. Keep these fast enough that the user never notices a delay.

Animations that block interaction are worse. If a user has to wait for a panel to finish sliding before they can click something inside it, the animation has become an obstacle. Motion should never stand between the user and their next action.

sections.title: Movement Principles
sections.body:
- Not everything needs an animated exit. Elements the user is moving away from, such as tooltips, hover cards, and dropdown menus, can disappear instantly. The user has already shifted their attention. Animate the exit only when it helps orient the user, like a panel closing or a dialog dismissing to reveal what's underneath.
- When you do animate exit, match the entrance. A panel that slides in from the right should slide back out to the right.
- Direction should match the action. Navigating deeper into content should feel like moving forward. Going back should feel like returning. This keeps the user oriented in the structure of the application.
- Contextual UI should feel connected to its trigger. A dropdown should expand from the button that opened it. A popover should appear near the element it describes. This doesn't apply to global UI like command palettes or toasts, which have their own fixed positions.

sections.title: Respecting User Preferences
sections.body: Some users experience motion sensitivity; animation that feels polished to one person can cause discomfort for another. When the OS reduced-motion setting is on, Astryx components change at once under a mouse or trackpad, and under a finger they cross-fade instead of moving: opacity only, in 200 ms or less. A value that changes in place, such as a progress fill, takes its new value at once under any pointer. Do the same in your own animations with `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, adding `(pointer: coarse)` for the touch cross-fade.

sections.title: Animate with motion tokens
Tune motion from the theme
sections.body:
A theme sets how motion feels with two knobs in `defineTheme`'s `motion`. They drive the CSS motion tokens, and `tempo` also times the springs of touch motion; those springs don't follow `character` yet. Every theme follows each person's Reduce Motion setting; no theme loosens it.

- `tempo` scales every motion duration: 1 is Astryx's own, 0.75 the quickest and 1.5 the slowest (values outside are clamped).
- `character` sets how lively motion is: `'crisp'` decelerates without overshoot, `'standard'` is Astryx's own, and `'expressive'` overshoots slightly on entrances and moves. Exits and fades never overshoot.

```
export const brandTheme = defineTheme({
  name: 'brand',
  motion: {tempo: 0.85, character: 'crisp'},
});
```

Some motion never follows the knobs, because it tracks a finger or the system: finger tracking, momentum and the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press model's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash (its release fade follows tempo), hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, the loops of busy indicators such as Spinner and Skeleton, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cross-fade.

Precedence, lowest to highest: the knobs, then a duration scale (`fast`, `medium`, `slow`, `ratio`) for the durations it sets, then explicit `tokens`. A theme with no `motion` renders exactly as before.

sections.title: Best Practices
sections.body:
- Animate transitions that involve spatial change: panels opening, content expanding, elements entering the screen.
- Use fast tokens for small, frequent interactions. Use medium tokens for larger transitions that rearrange the layout.
- Honor reduced motion preferences at the OS level.

- Let hover states or high-frequency interactions feel like they're lagging behind the user.
- Let animation delay when a user can interact with new content. The transition should complete before (or not block) the next action.
- Move elements in ways that contradict where they came from or where they're going.

docs.title: Styling overview
docs.description: How to set up CSS — exact imports for three paths: plain, Tailwind, and StyleX for your own code — plus the stylesheet each Astryx package ships.

sections.title: Pick a path
sections.body: All three load the same prebuilt Astryx stylesheets, resolve to the same design tokens, and support theming and dark mode. None of them compiles Astryx package source. You can mix them in one app.

sections.title: Plain CSS
Tailwind
StyleX for your own code
Other Astryx packages
Further reading
sections.body:
- {@link namespace:styling} — xstyle, className, data-attribute selectors, design tokens in code.
- {@link namespace:styling-libraries} — Tailwind bridge details, Panda, Chakra, MUI, CSS Modules, and non-CSS token resolution.
- {@link generic:use-a-theme} — applying themes, dark mode, nested themes. {@link generic:author-a-theme} — defineTheme, overrides, production builds.

docs.title: Icons
docs.description: Built-in meanings available in the design system. These adapt to the active theme's icons.

sections.title: Available Names
sections.body: Components that accept an icon prop use IconType: either a built-in meaning string or a direct SVG component. The built-in meanings below are resolved through the global icon registry.

sections.title: Custom Icons
sections.body:
For icons not in the built-in list, pass an SVG component directly. Any ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>> works; Icon applies size and color styling automatically.

```
import { PhotoIcon } from '@heroicons/react/24/outline';
import { HeartIcon } from 'lucide-react';

<Icon icon={PhotoIcon} size="lg" />
<Icon icon={HeartIcon} color="error" />
```

Icon Variants
Component and Library Icons
Component Icon Slots

docs.title: Is my Astryx code good?
docs.description: Check whether a product surface fits its app and uses Astryx well, require evidence for every claim, and improve it with a repeatable agent review.

sections.title: Understand the app
sections.body:
Do not judge a file or surface in isolation. First learn the app context that makes a pattern correct, inconsistent, or incomplete.

- Name what the app is for, who uses it, and the task this surface helps them complete.
- Trace where the surface sits: its route, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, and the page or block pattern it is meant to use.
- Inspect sibling surfaces that do the same or adjacent jobs. Record their shared headers, actions, layout primitives, spacing, density, states, and narrow-screen behavior.
- Read project guidance, including the root and relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files. Record app-owned wrapper components and intentional app conventions.
- Record the installed `@astryxdesign/core`, `@astryxdesign/cli`, and integration-package versions from the project manifest and lockfile. Run the installed invocation of `{@command component --list}` to see core and integration components, then inspect app-owned wrappers that do not appear in that catalog.
- List the real data states, roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile or narrow-width needs that affect the task.

Keep this context with the review. Mark anything you could not learn as `not inspected`. Do not flag a documented, intentional app convention merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify that the user task and accessibility requirements still work.

sections.title: Choose the review
sections.body:
Review one exact revision and one named product surface, route, or component in its app context. Pick the smallest review that can answer your question.

If all you have is one source file, run the source check anyway and use any project context that is available. Report clear source blockers; list missing app purpose, route, sibling patterns, shell, theme and density, installed components and versions, real states and roles, locale and mobile needs, revision, runnable app, rendered states, and project checks; and do not call the full product good.

`astryx` in this guide means the project's installed CLI invocation, such as its local binary or existing package script. If the project has no installed invocation, report that evidence gap instead of downloading a different CLI version for the review.

A screenshot can prove a visible result, but it cannot prove which imports, components, or styles produced it. Source alone cannot prove responsive behavior, interaction, color modes, or whether an asset loads. Mark anything outside the supplied evidence as `not inspected`.

sections.title: Apply the shared rubric
sections.body:
Mark each category `good`, `needs work`, or `not inspected`. Cite the route, sibling surface, project guidance, theme, component catalog, or user requirement behind every context-dependent result; cite a file and line for every source result; and name the rendered state for every visual result. Never turn missing evidence into a pass. A blocker is a finding that prevents the surface from building, rendering, operating, letting the target user complete the task, or meeting an accessibility requirement. Other departures from the rubric are `needs work`.

Before calling a pattern custom or wrong, compare sibling surfaces and the installed component catalog. Reuse an app-owned wrapper or integration component when it already owns the job. A documented app convention is not a finding merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify the user's task and accessibility requirements.

Keep a native element when its semantics are necessary and Astryx has no equivalent. Common examples are a `form` that provides native submission, `input type="hidden"` for native form state, and an `img` when no general Astryx image component fits.

- Compare the route with sibling surfaces that do the same job. Identify the app's shared header, actions, shell, page pattern, spacing, and density before judging the target.
- Inspect every JSX opening tag. Moving raw HTML behind a PascalCase helper does not make the underlying pattern an Astryx component.
- Count every raw SVG element used as an icon, including `svg`, `path`, `circle`, `rect`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `ellipse`, and `g`. For an inline SVG helper, count its raw SVG elements once in the helper definition, not again at each render. Count each icon-library component rendered directly outside an Astryx icon surface.
- Look up a possible replacement with `{@command component <Name> --dense}`. Do not invent a component or prop that the installed version does not provide.
- Run the installed `{@command component --list}` and inspect app-owned wrappers before rebuilding a pattern. Prefer the component the app or one of its installed integrations already uses for the job.
- Inspect every `stylex.cr

sections.title: Collect the evidence
sections.body:
- Record the exact revision, named surface, route, and source files in scope. If the files are outside version control, record a content hash for each file and say that no project revision was available.
- Write down the app's purpose, target users, surface task, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, expected page pattern, and sibling surfaces used for comparison.
- Record project guidance, theme, density, installed Astryx and integration versions, the relevant output of `{@command component --list}`, and app-owned wrappers or conventions.
- List the states and context that matter, including real data shapes, roles and permissions, empty, loading, error, long content, interaction, narrow width, wide width, supported color modes, locales, and RTL behavior when they apply.
- Run the product and capture each named rendered state. Use screenshots or a live browser result for visible claims, and follow the target user task from entry to completion.
- Run the build, type check, tests, and accessibility checks. Keep their commands and results with the review.
- For each Astryx component whose replacement, prop, or composition is in question, read `{@command component <Name> --dense}`.

sections.title: Ask an agent
sections.body:
Start with a read-only pass so the original findings stay visible. Replace every angle-bracket value in this prompt.

```
Evaluate how well <surface> at <revision> fits <app> and uses Astryx. Do not edit files during this first pass.

`astryx` below means the project's installed CLI invocation, such as its local binary or existing package script. If none is installed, report that evidence gap instead of downloading a different version.

Before evaluating:
1. Read `astryx docs is-my-code-good --full`.
2. Read the root and relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files plus other project guidance. State what the app is for, who uses it, and the task this surface supports.
3. Trace the surface's route, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, and expected page or block pattern.
4. Inspect at least two sibling surfaces that do the same or adjacent jobs. Record their shared headers, actions, layout, spacing, density, states, and narrow-screen behavior.
5. Record the app's theme, density, app-owned wrappers, and documented intentional conventions.
6. Read the project manifest and lockfile for the installed Astryx, CLI, and integration versions. Run `astryx component --list`, then identify relevant integration components and app-owned wrappers.
7. List the real data states, roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile or narrow-width needs.
8. Inspect every source file in scope and its public imports.
9. Run `astryx component <Name> --dense` for each Astryx component whose replacement, prop, or composition you question.
10. Read `astryx docs spacing --full` and the target component's docs before mapping a literal spacing value to a prop or token.
11. Render every supplied state at narrow and wide widths and in each supported color mode.
12. Read the build, type-check, test, and accessibility-check results.

If only source is supplied, continue with a source check. Report blockers visible in the source, list every missing app-context and product-evidence item, and do not call the full product good. Do not leave the blocker list empty only because no checks were supplied.

Judge the code against the app as well as Astryx. Ask whether it matches sibling sur

sections.title: Verify, improve, and repeat
sections.body:
- Reject a `good` result without app-context, source, and rendered evidence. Open every cited route, sibling file, guidance file, and source location, and reproduce every named visible state.
- Check that documented intentional app conventions were not flagged merely for differing from a generic pattern, and that context the reviewer could not learn stayed `not inspected`.
- Fix task-completion, build, functional, and accessibility blockers first.
- Reuse the app shell, page pattern, wrappers, and installed integration components before replacing unnecessary raw elements, direct icons, and custom styles.
- Follow the target user task again, render the full state set, and rerun the project checks.
- Repeat the read-only review on the new revision. Keep the first report so the improvement and every remaining tradeoff stay visible.

For an integration template, finish with the scored package and copy workflow in {@link generic:grade-template-with-agent}. Ordinary product code stops with the evidence-backed category report and does not receive a template publication grade.

docs.title: Browser support
docs.description: What browsers Astryx targets, which modern platform features it depends on, and how to support older browsers for your own audience.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
Astryx is built on modern web platform features: the [`Popover`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) API, CSS anchor positioning, and CSS `light-dark()`. These let components stay small, accessible, and dependency-free, but they also set a floor on which browsers render everything correctly.

A design system does not own its traffic; the products built on it do. Their audiences range from evergreen-Chrome-only internal tools to public sites with meaningful older-Safari share. So Astryx does not declare a single hard browser floor the way an app would. Instead it defines tiers that describe what works at each level, and hands the final decision to you. Pick the tier that matches your audience.

sections.title: Support Tiers
sections.body: Astryx officially supports Tier 1 and Tier 2. Tier 3 is best-effort: components will not crash, but positioning and theming may degrade.

sections.title: Which Features Set the Floor
sections.body:
Only three modern features carry a browser requirement. Everything else Astryx uses (`:has()`, `color-mix()`, container queries, the `<dialog>` element) has been widely available since 2023 or earlier and needs no special handling.

The gap that matters is between Tier 1 and Tier 2: the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` reached wide availability well before anchor positioning. So in Tier 2 browsers, layered surfaces open and dismiss correctly; they just are not positioned. This is the one feature most consumers will need to reason about.

sections.title: Which Components Are Affected
sections.body:
Any component that opens a menu, popover, tooltip, or dropdown carries the browser requirement: it renders that surface in an overlay positioned against its trigger. That includes:

- Tooltip, HoverCard, and Popover, and any prop that shows one (such as the Button `tooltip`)
- DropdownMenu, MoreMenu, and ContextMenu
- Selector, MultiSelector, ComplexSelector, Typeahead, and PowerSearch (dropdown surfaces)
- DateInput, DateRangeInput, and DateTimeInput (calendar popovers)
- Tokenizer (suggestion menu)
- The overflow and flyout menus in Breadcrumbs, TabList, TopNav, and SideNav
- Carousel (anchored controls)

If your product opens no menus, popovers, tooltips, or dropdowns, it has no anchor-positioning requirement; it needs only `light-dark()` (Tier 2 and up) for correct theme colors. Page layout, typography, forms, buttons, cards, and tables work down to Tier 2 with no special handling.

sections.title: What Astryx Guarantees
sections.body:
- Components never throw on missing platform APIs. Where a browser lacks the `Popover` API, layers fall back to plain visibility instead of crashing.
- Tier 1 and Tier 2 are officially supported and tested.
- Non-layered components render correctly down to Tier 2.

- Astryx does not guarantee correct layer positioning below Tier 1 (anchor positioning). Closing that gap for a Tier 2 audience is a consumer choice; see below.
- Astryx does not ship a `light-dark()` fallback, so theme colors are not guaranteed below Tier 2.

sections.title: The On-Screen Keyboard
sections.body:
On a phone, the components that respond to the on-screen keyboard, a fully expanded `height='tall'` BottomSheet and ChatLayout's composer, measure it the same way: the layout viewport's height minus the visual viewport's height times its scale. Where the visual viewport shrinks for the keyboard, as in Safari on iOS in the browser and as a home-screen app, in Firefox for Android and in Chrome on Android, they keep the focused field and the surface around it above the keyboard and leave the page where it was. If Firefox for Android pans to the field, they put the page back within a couple of frames.

In Chrome on Android, ChatLayout’s composer rides the keyboard as Gboard slides it up and down. A Tall BottomSheet’s focused field rides the keyboard as Gboard slides it up, and as Gboard slides it down after the field loses focus. The scroll room stays until the keyboard is down. A hide Chrome reports late, such as Back, which keeps the focus, rides down from Chrome’s report. When the keyboard is reported, the sheet places the field just above it in that same frame, so Chrome has no covered field to pan to; if Chrome pans anyway, the sheet puts the page back when that pan ends. Chrome follows your viewport setting, which Astryx documents and never sets: your app owns its viewport `<meta>` element. By default (`interactive-widget=resizes-visual`) Chrome lays the keyboard over the page and pans to a focused field elsewhere on the page. With `interactive-widget=resizes-content` it shrinks the layout viewport instead, so content anchored to the bottom sits above the keyboard, and those components measure no keyboard and change nothing: the browser has already made the room.

```
<meta
  name="viewport"
  content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, interactive-widget=resizes-content" />
```

sections.title: Supporting Older Browsers
How These Tiers Move Over Time
sections.body:
The tiers are rolling, not frozen to specific versions. They track the Web Baseline year:

- Tier 1 tracks the current Baseline year.
- Tier 2 tracks Baseline minus two years.
- Tier 3 is everything older, and remains best-effort.

This is not an arbitrary window: Baseline − 2 is close to where anchor positioning stops being available while the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` still are, so the tier boundary tracks a real capability edge, not a guessed date. The version floors above are reviewed and advanced roughly once a year as new Baseline years land. Always feature-detect rather than hardcoding version numbers, so your app adapts automatically as the platform moves.
